chapter_theme: Civakan, by a pool outside Hemamapuram, longs for Gandharvadattai, reasons that she lives, then checks his desire with the thought that lust leads to hell where only the Jina is refuge; Prince Vijayan meets him, receives a false name, sees him shoot down a mango, and brings him to King Tadamittan, who reads his archer's marks and makes him teacher of the princes; the section ends in a spring grove where he strings a garland.

cast.role: the hero, here a stranger at Hemamapuram hiding his name
Civakan's first wife, a Vidyadhara's daughter, of whom he thinks (called தத்தை in 1626)
prince of Hemamapuram, son of Tadamittan and Nalinai, who befriends Civakan
king of Hemamapuram, Vijayan's father (written தட மித்தன் in 1635)
the four other youths of the king's house whom Civakan teaches with Vijayan

1629.reading: Civakan, alone by the pool, wonders whether his garlanded beloved, withered and darkened by grief, now lets tears from both eyes run between her breasts until they make a pond where herons dive.
1629.nuance: The beloved is not named in the verse; 1626 has just named தத்தை, so this is Gandharvadattai. The hyperbole of a tear-pond for herons turns his worry into a picture of her body.
1629.event: Civakan, by the pool outside Hemamapuram, imagines Gandharvadattai weeping for him.

1630.reading: He recalls the look she drank him in with at their first meeting at the wedding, scooping him up with her eyes as if they were hands, and says that one look melts his life.
1630.nuance: The eyes are made into hands that scoop and drink (நொண்டு கொண்டு பருகிய), a bold image of looking as consuming.

1631.reading: He reasons that if his beloved's life had left her body his own would have perished with it, so she has come to no harm; and besides, is she not skilled in the Vidyadhara arts?
1631.nuance: The comfort is an inference from the lovers' shared life, backed by her magic (விஞ்சை): as a Vidyadhara's daughter she can guard herself. He uses this to quiet the fear of 1627 that she might die in the fire of parting.

claims.claim: the lives of true lovers are so joined that one cannot die without the other

1632.reading: He says that when love grows too strong what one has learned gives no help, as the eye cannot see the collyrium within it, and so his heart keeps fearing harm for the bee-like one who has settled on the pollen.
1632.nuance: The collyrium simile: what is nearest the eye is what it cannot see; so learning fails a man in love exactly where it is needed. The last two lines are hard to construe; whether the bee is she or his own heart is not certain.

claims.claim: when love is excessive, learning gives no help

1633.reading: He then reflects that the evil deeds that come from fierce lust for the beauty of garlanded women make one writhe in hell, and that there no one but the Omniscient can be a refuge.
1633.nuance: The turn is sudden: from longing for his own wife he passes to the doctrine that desire itself breeds தீவினை. அறிவன், the Omniscient, is the Jina, as in 1241-1247. Line 3 is corrupt in the edition (a lost letter in பறவைத் தோ?நரகத்து), so the exact picture of hell is lost.

claims.claim: fierce lust for women's beauty brings evil deeds that torment one in hell
in hell only the Omniscient Jina is a refuge

1634.reading: Turning his swelling, desire-driven mind back, the bull-like hero enjoys instead the beauty of the flower-crowded pool and stays on there.
1634.nuance: The reflection of 1633 is acted on at once: desire is not killed but redirected to the pleasure of the scene, a householder's restraint rather than a renouncer's.
1634.event: Civakan masters his longing and stays by the pool.

1635.reading: The narrator introduces Vijayan, born in a palace full of treasure where enemies come to submit, to King Tadamittan of hard wars and to Nalinai of noble chastity, a prince made perfect in fortune and all else.

1636.reading: Vijayan, of the fierce horse-drawn chariot, whose fame the world praises, a sea of learning, enters the fragrant grove, sees the young hero and joins him.
1636.event: Prince Vijayan comes into the grove and meets Civakan.

1637.reading: Asked whether he lives here or which land, town and name are his, Civakan gives a land, town and name other than his own; the narrator says that though he set up a falsehood, the fame-loving hero did so in a way that was no lie.
1637.nuance: Civakan is hiding from Kattiyangaran; the narrator feels bound to defend the false name. The construal of line 4 (பொய்ந்நாட் டேனும் பொய்யல ஆற்றால்) is not certain: it may mean that the lie harmed no one, or that the hero kept truth in conduct while hiding his name.
1637.event: Vijayan asks Civakan who he is, and Civakan gives a false land, town and name.

claims.claim: a falsehood told without harm, by one who loves honour, is not a lie

1638.reading: Vijayan, his heart overflowing, resolves to bring this spear-bearer to the king for his great worth, for not even Indra is his equal, and to find a way to keep company with him.
1638.event: Vijayan resolves to take Civakan to his father.

1639.reading: Vijayan tells him that this land, this city and this house are now his own, and its people his kin, and Civakan accepts, saying let it be so.
1639.nuance: The offer answers the false name of 1637: the stranger who gave no true home is given one.
1639.event: Vijayan offers Civakan his land and house as his own, and Civakan accepts.

1640.reading: The king's son tries to shoot down a mango, misses again and again with his bright arrows, and stops; the hero takes the bow and with one arrow brings down the nectar-dripping fruit.
1640.event: Vijayan fails to shoot a mango; Civakan shoots it down.

1641.reading: As the arrow and the fruit come down to earth within reach of the bow, the prince, seeing it, goes to the man who shot without moving from his place, embraces him and speaks.
1641.nuance: The point of the shot is that arrow and fruit fall back at the archer's feet; 1642's சென்ற கோல் போந்த ஆறு says the same.
1641.event: Vijayan embraces Civakan after the shot.

1642.reading: Marvelling at how he took the bow, fitted the arrow, set his eye, held his stone-hard shoulders, loosed the shaft and how the arrow came back, Vijayan calls him a god of the bow.

1643.reading: Vijayan says that of Rama, who pierced the seven sal trees, people only say he was skilled, while none has seen it, and resolving to make this man glad without strain, he leaves the grove and takes him to the palace.
1643.nuance: Rama's feat is set aside as hearsay (இசையலாற் கண்டதில்லை) against what Vijayan has just seen with his own eyes; the epic rates seen skill over a famous story.
1643.event: Vijayan brings Civakan from the grove to the palace.

1644.reading: After easing the toil of the road, the diamond-breasted prince tells the king of the stranger's skill, and the king, glad of the words, greets the great-bowed man with high courtesy and calls him a beloved young man.
1644.event: Vijayan tells his father of Civakan, and the king welcomes him.

1645.reading: Seeing on his hand the marks of the archer's art, the bowstring scar and the lines likened to elephant hide and small fish, the king calls him a king of the arrow.
1645.nuance: The king reads the hand by a learned system of marks (இலக்கணக் கிடக்கை); the technical terms of line 1 (கிலுத்தம், பரம்) and the measure of three fingers are not clear to me.
1645.event: The king reads the archer's marks on Civakan's hand.

1646.reading: The king praises him: among bowmen, where an unfailing master stands, he has come to silence those who say that none but the Vidyadharas of the silver mountain is his equal on earth.
1646.nuance: Line 1 (அமோகமா ஆசான்) is obscure; it may name a famed archery master or call Civakan an unfailing teacher.

1647.reading: The king says his son has not mastered the bow, and that besides him four others have not grown to excellence, and asks the victorious guest to grant them his skill; the prince agrees, and from that day they train.
1647.nuance: விருந்தினன் may call the prince a novice or refer to Civakan as the guest; the request turns the hidden prince into a teacher of princes.
1647.event: The king asks Civakan to teach archery to his son and four others, and Civakan agrees.

1648.reading: The pupils cling to his lotus feet in love and never leave his shadow; he makes them able to do whatever they think of, and they keep near him as men near a fire, neither too close nor too far; one day he goes out to a grove that shines like a bride.
1648.nuance: அழலிற் சாராது அகலாது ஒழுக is the image of Kural 691, in other words, for courtiers with a king; here it is the pupils' conduct toward a teacher.
1648.event: The princes train under Civakan; one day he goes into a flowering grove.

1649.reading: In the grove the vengai blooms like a gold necklace strung on moss-green cord, like white cloth dipped in water and thrown over, the azhinjil drips honey, and the punku trees wear red-headed, white-spotted puffed blossom.

1650.reading: The vakulam, the tall champak, the kongu and other trees have flowered, some likened to pots and chariot wheels, the cock-spur buds have opened, and the patiri and white kadamba wear their round blossoms.
1650.nuance: The similes of line 1 (pots, chariot wheels) are hard to fix to particular trees.

1651.reading: Mullai buds as if laughing to tempt the wild cat, kanthal opening like a cobra's spread hood, kuravam buds like quail, and the talavam with buds like a dancer's red sharp teeth fill the grove.

1652.reading: With those flowers and others, and fallen jackfruit segments, he strings a garland by the rules of the art with the tips of his fingers, so that it looks like gems, pearls, coral and gold strung together and even the gods marvel.
1652.nuance: The garland-making is one more of the hero's arts done by the book (நன்மை நூலின் நயம் தோன்ற), after archery; it prepares the next scene.
1652.event: Civakan strings a garland of the grove's flowers.

links.note: 1627 fears she will die in the fire of parting; 1631 argues she cannot have, since he lives.
links.teaches: Together they show the hero answering his own fear with an argument rather than news, using the lovers' shared life as evidence, so that separation grief turns into reasoning.

links.note: Kemasari cited his doctrine that lovers' lives become one to reproach him for leaving her; he now uses the same doctrine to reassure himself about Gandharvadattai.
links.teaches: Held together, the verses show one premise serving opposite ends: for the wife he has just left it proves his desertion wrong, for the absent first wife it proves she is safe, so the doctrine binds him only where it comforts.

links.note: The couplet calls the bond with the girl that of body and life; the epic draws an inference from it during separation.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's simile into a test a separated lover can run, that one life cannot end while the other goes on, and so shows the image used as reassurance rather than praise.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's settled formula, so the hero's inference rests on a known saying about lovers
gains.b: the couplet gains a situation of separation and a consequence drawn from its image, which it never states

links.note: Both say lust breeds the evil that ends in hell; Manimekalai puts it in an ascetic's sermon on the five things to shun, the Cintamani in the hero's thought about his own wife.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic uses the rule to say lust must be renounced and only ascetics manage it, while the Jain epic lets a married hero apply it mid-romance and simply turn his mind, so the same doctrine works there as a householder's brake, not a call to the robe.

links.note: The couplet allows a falsehood that yields faultless good; the narrator excuses the hero's false name in similar terms.
links.teaches: The epic gives the couplet's exception a concrete case, a fugitive prince hiding his name from a usurper, and shows a narrator reaching for the exception to keep his hero truthful.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised rule under which its awkward excuse of the hero's lie can be judged
gains.b: the couplet gains a test case where the 'good' is the liar's own safety, which leaves open whether its strict condition is met

links.note: The couplet tells courtiers to keep near a king like men warming at a fire; the epic gives the same fire conduct to pupils with their teacher.
links.teaches: The epic moves the rule from court to schoolroom, and since the teacher is a hidden king, the princes unknowingly keep the courtier's rule toward a real king.

gains.a: the epic verse gains the couplet's reason for the distance: the one served can burn as well as warm
gains.b: the couplet gains an application beyond kingship, to any one whose favour is sought, here a master of an art

source_issues: 1633 line 3: the edition prints a lost or unreadable letter (பறவைத் தோ?நரகத்து); the word before நரகத்து cannot be fixed.
1636, 1637, 1641, 1642, 1644-1649, 1651, 1652: stanzas printed as eight half-lines, joined into four lines by the build.
1645 line 1 (கிலுத்தங்கூர்ப் பரங்கள்) and 1646 line 1 (அமோகமா வாசான்) are obscure, possibly corrupt.
